title: Root System
summary: The root system is the descending part of the plant axis, developed from the radicle. Roots are non-green, have no nodes, internodes, leaves or buds, and are positively geotropic, positively hydrotropic and negatively phototropic. Tap root system: the primary root persists and gives lateral roots (dicots: gram, mustard, carrot, neem); gives strong anchorage. Fibrous root system: the primary root is short-lived and a cluster of fibre-like roots arises from the base of the stem (monocots: wheat, maize, grasses); shallow. Adventitious roots arise from any part of the plant other than the radicle (nodes of money plant, banyan branches, stem cuttings of rose, stem base of monocots).

From the tip: root cap (protects the apical meristem; loose root pocket in aquatic plants Pistia and water hyacinth), region of meristematic cells (dermatogen gives epiblema and root cap; periblem gives cortex; plerome gives stele; calyptrogen forms the cap in monocots; the quiescent centre is a group of inactive cells that becomes active if the meristem is damaged), region of elongation (cells enlarge and the root grows in length) and region of maturation (root hair zone absorbs water and mineral salts; permanent zone gives lateral roots and anchors).

Tap root modifications for food storage: conical (broad base tapering to the tip; carrot), fusiform (swollen in the middle and tapering at both ends; radish), napiform (spherical at the base and tapering sharply; turnip) and tuberous (fleshy with no definite shape; four o'clock plant). Adventitious root modifications: tuberous (sweet potato), fasciculated (cluster of swollen roots; dahlia), nodulose (only tips swollen; mango ginger), moniliform (beaded; grasses), annulated (looks like discs; ipecac); assimilatory roots (green aerial roots that photosynthesise; Tinospora); epiphytic roots (with velamen tissue to absorb moisture; Vanda orchid); pneumatophores or respiratory roots (grow upward out of water in marshy mangroves such as Rhizophora for gas exchange); sucking roots or haustoria (parasite Cuscuta draws food from the host phloem); prop roots (hang from branches for support; banyan); stilt roots (from lower nodes; sugarcane, screwpine); climbing roots (money plant, betel); clinging roots (epiphytes); floating roots (Jussiaea, aquatic, spongy for buoyancy and respiration). Functions of roots: anchorage, absorption and conduction of water and minerals, and special functions through modification.

Dicot root (gram): epiblema (single layer, with unicellular root hairs); cortex (parenchyma, stores food); endodermis (barrel-shaped cells with Casparian strips; passage cells opposite the protoxylem lack the strips and allow water to pass); pericycle (origin of lateral roots, vascular cambium and cork cambium); radial vascular bundles with xylem exarch (protoxylem towards the periphery, metaxylem towards the centre), two to six xylem patches (diarch to hexarch); conjunctive tissue between xylem and phloem; pith absent or very small. Monocot root (maize): similar, but xylem is polyarch (many bundles), pith is large, there is no cambium and no secondary growth.

Differences: dicot root has 2-6 vascular bundles, pericycle forms lateral roots, cambium and cork cambium, secondary growth present, pith small; monocot root has many bundles, pericycle forms only lateral roots, no cambium, no secondary growth, large pith. Lateral roots arise endogenously from the pericycle opposite the protoxylem; the number of lateral roots equals the number of xylem bundles.
## Secondary growth in a dicot root

Only in dicots. Strips of vascular cambium form from conjunctive tissue inside the phloem and from pericycle cells outside the protoxylem; they join into a wavy ring that becomes circular. The cambium cuts secondary phloem towards the outside and secondary xylem towards the inside. Secondary tissue opposite the protoxylem forms primary medullary rays. Cork cambium (phellogen) arises from the pericycle and forms cork (phellem) outside and secondary cortex (phelloderm) inside; phellogen, phellem and phelloderm together form the periderm, which protects the root; the epiblema, cortex and endodermis are sloughed off.

objective: Match: (a) Prop roots (b) Haustorium (c) Sweet potato (d) Floating roots with (i) Storage (ii) Jussiaea (iii) Banyan (iv) Cuscuta.
Name the modification: (a) Rhizophora roots coming up from the marsh (b) Roots of Cuscuta.
Fill in the blanks: (a) The lateral roots arise from the ______. (b) The number of xylem patches in a dicot root is ______ to six.
State true or false: (a) The cambium is absent in a monocot root. (b) Roots are positively phototropic.
(a) True. (b) False – roots are negatively phototropic.
Name the type of root modification and one example for storage: (a) swollen in the middle (b) spherical at the base.
Name the layers formed by the cork cambium on its outer and inner sides.
Name the two regions of the maturation zone of the root.
Root hair (piliferous) region and the permanent region.
In a tetrarch root, how many lateral roots form in one row?
Four, equal to the number of xylem bundles.
vsa: Identify the modified root in the following: (1) Rhizophora (2) Cuscuta (3) Banyan (4) Sugarcane (5) Money plant.
(1) Pneumatophores. (2) Haustoria (sucking roots). (3) Prop roots. (4) Stilt roots. (5) Climbing roots.
Differentiate between tap root and fibrous root systems (two points).
A tap root system has a persistent primary root with branches, going deep and giving strong anchorage; a fibrous system has a cluster of thin roots from the stem base, which is shallow.
A group of inactive cells between the root cap and the active meristem; they become active when the meristem is damaged.
Endodermal cells opposite the protoxylem without Casparian strips, through which water and salts pass from the cortex into the xylem.
Anchoring the plant in the soil and absorbing water and mineral salts.
Why are carrot, radish and turnip considered roots?
They are fleshy, have no nodes or buds and bear lateral roots; they store food and develop from the radicle.
What is meant by exarch xylem?
The protoxylem lies towards the periphery and the metaxylem towards the centre.
The protective layers of phellogen, phellem and phelloderm formed in secondary growth.
sa: Give any three differences between a dicot root and a monocot root.
Dicot root: 2-6 xylem bundles, small pith, secondary growth present. Monocot root: many bundles (polyarch), large pith, no secondary growth.
Describe the regions of the root tip.
Root cap protects the apex; meristematic zone divides; elongation zone makes the root longer; maturation zone has root hairs for absorption and a permanent zone producing lateral roots.
Write about the modifications of tap root for food storage.
Conical (carrot), fusiform (radish), napiform (turnip) and tuberous (four o'clock plant): they are swollen and fleshy for storing food.

They arise endogenously from the pericycle opposite the protoxylem; the cells divide to form a hump which pushes through the endodermis and cortex and emerges as a branch; the number of lateral roots equals the number of xylem bundles.
Describe the adventitious roots modified for support.
Prop roots (banyan) hang from branches and support them; stilt roots (sugarcane) grow obliquely from the lower nodes; climbing roots (money plant) clasp the support.
What are pneumatophores? Where are they found and what is their function?
Respiratory roots that grow vertically upward out of marshy water with minute pores; found in mangroves such as Rhizophora; they help in gaseous exchange.
la: Identify the modified adventitious root in the following: (1) Rhizophora (2) Cuscuta (3) Banyan (4) Sugarcane (5) Money plant. Mention the function of each.
(1) Pneumatophores: gas exchange. (2) Haustoria: absorb food from the host. (3) Prop roots: support. (4) Stilt roots: support. (5) Climbing roots: attach to the support.
Describe the secondary growth in a dicot root.

A cambium ring forms from the conjunctive tissue and pericycle; it adds secondary phloem outside and secondary xylem inside; cork cambium arises from the pericycle and forms cork and secondary cortex; the periderm protects the root and the epiblema, cortex and endodermis peel off.
Describe the internal structure of a dicot root.
Epiblema with root hairs, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips and passage cells, pericycle, radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem, conjunctive tissue and a small pith.
Explain the adventitious root modifications for storage, photosynthesis and absorption of moisture.
Tuberous (sweet potato), fasciculated (dahlia), nodulose (mango ginger), moniliform and annulated store food; assimilatory roots photosynthesise; epiphytic roots absorb moisture using velamen.
